Advice from a  real psychologist  that will probably hurt your 
feelings but may fix your high functioning anxiety.

1. If you can only stop working once you’re completely exhausted, that’s not dedication. That’s anxiety deciding when you’re allowed to rest.

2. If making a mistake feels like proof you’re not good enough, that’s not having high standards. That’s tying your worth to your performance.

3. If you feel guilty the moment you sit down, that’s not proof you should be doing more.That’s a learned association between being productive and being worthy.

4. If you reread the same email six times and still can’t take it in, that’s not a discipline problem. That’s stress disrupting the prefrontal brain systems that support attention and working memory.

5. If you notice your partner’s mood changing and immediately assume you’ve done something wrong, that’s not proof you’re reading them accurately.
That’s threat monitoring.

6. If saying yes makes you feel relieved, that’s not always a sign you made the right decision. Sometimes you’ve just escaped the discomfort of saying no.

7. If you need to feel completely calm before you speak up, that’s not always preparation. That’s avoidance.

Psychology says feeling relieved isn’t always the same as feeling better. Sometimes you’ve just done what anxiety wanted. Short term relief keeps anxiety going. You feel better briefly, but the pattern repeats.

You can get through the whole day being “fine”… then snap at someone you love over something small.

🎨worry__lines

You brushed off the disappointment.
Said yes when you wanted to say no.
Stayed busy so you didn’t have to notice how overwhelmed you felt.

And by bedtime, you have very little patience left.

When you’re used to being the capable one, acknowledging your feelings can feel like another task you don’t have time for.

Start small…
“What am I feeling?”
“What’s been difficult today?”
“What do I need next?”

Sometimes that means a boundary. Sometimes a conversation, a cry, or leaving something unfinished so you can rest.

You don’t have to analyse every feeling or fix it immediately. You can make room for it and still choose what you do next.

Save this for the days when “I’m fine” is doing a lot of heavy lifting. 🤍

Here they are 👇⁠
⁠
1. You replay conversations for hours afterwards.⁠
You keep wondering if you said the wrong thing.⁠
⁠
2. You can’t truly relax, even when there’s nothing to do.⁠
Rest feels uncomfortable instead of restorative.⁠
⁠
3. You always expect the worst-case scenario.⁠
Your brain constantly scans for what could go wrong.⁠
⁠
4. You feel guilty whenever you say no.⁠
Other people’s disappointment feels like your responsibility.⁠
⁠
5. You overprepare for everything.⁠
You tell yourself you’re just being organised, but you’re terrified of making a mistake.⁠
⁠
6. You struggle to switch your brain off at night.⁠
Bedtime becomes your brain’s favourite time to analyse everything.⁠
⁠
7. You look calm on the outside but feel overwhelmed inside.⁠
Everyone thinks you’re coping because you’re so capable.⁠
⁠
8. You constantly need reassurance that you’ve done enough.⁠
One compliment rarely outweighs one criticism.⁠
⁠
9. You stay busy because slowing down feels uncomfortable.⁠
Productivity has become your way of feeling safe.⁠
⁠
10. You feel responsible for everyone else’s emotions.⁠
You automatically manage other people’s moods before your own.⁠
⁠

Stress eating is often an attempt to regulate how you feel.

So before you tell yourself “don’t eat”, try this:

Put both feet on the floor.
Take one slow breath out longer than you breathe in.
Name what you’re actually feeling…stressed, lonely, angry, overwhelmed, rejected, exhausted.

Then ask “What does my nervous system need right now?”

Food might still be what you choose.

But the goal is to stop food being your only way to feel better.

High sensitivity is linked with a trait called sensory processing sensitivity.

It’s not a disorder.

It’s associated with processing experiences deeply, noticing subtle changes and becoming overwhelmed more easily by sensory and emotional input.

So she didn’t just notice what people said.

She noticed the change in their tone.
The look on their face.
The tension in the room.
The possibility that she had disappointed someone.

And she learned that being the “good girl” helped her feel safe.

Be helpful. Get it right. Don’t be difficult.
Don’t upset anyone. Never give people a reason to criticise you.

She started feeling responsible for other people’s feelings, anticipating every possible problem and putting enormous pressure on herself to get everything right.

This is why her anxiety doesn’t always look like falling apart.

It looks like high achievement. Perfectionism.
People-pleasing. Overpreparing. Never switching off.

She appears capable because she is capable.

But internally, she’s replaying conversations, second-guessing decisions, predicting worst-case scenarios and wondering whether she has done enough.

The same sensitivity that helps her notice more, care deeply and perform at a high level also means she is processing more.

So now, even the life she worked so hard to create can feel overwhelming.

Her mind never stops. Small decisions feel heavy.
Rest brings guilt. And every new responsibility feels like one more thing she cannot afford to get wrong.

The hardest part about anxiety often isn't the anxiety itself. It's the fight with it. ⁠
⁠
When your brain detects anxiety, it naturally wants to get rid of it. So you distract yourself, seek reassurance, overthink, avoid, or tell yourself to "calm down."⁠
⁠
The problem is that every time you treat anxiety like a threat that must be eliminated, your brain learns that it really is dangerous. And next time, it comes back louder.⁠
⁠
Acceptance doesn't mean liking anxiety or giving up. It means making space for the feeling instead of wrestling with it. You can notice it, breathe through it, and continue doing what matters to you, even while it's there.⁠
⁠
That's how your nervous system gradually learns "This feeling is uncomfortable, but it isn't dangerous."⁠
⁠
Ironically, the less you fight anxiety, the less power it has over you.⁠

Science shows about 80% of our daily thoughts are somewhat negative. It’s not a flaw, it’s your mind acting like an overprotective friend, always scanning for problems.

Humans hate uncertainty. If we don’t know how something will turn out, we would rather predict something negative happening rather than sit with the uncertainty of not knowing.

This means we naturally ‘fuse’ with negative thoughts more easily than positive ones.

But what is ‘fusion’?...

Thoughts are just words in your mind. Fusion happens when you believe them as reality.

‘Defusion’ means noticing them just as just words, not facts.

Don’t fight your thoughts because they get louder.

Instead, label them...

“I’m noticing the thought that I’m not good enough.”

This creates space to choose your next move.

High sensitivity is linked to a temperament trait called sensory processing sensitivity (SPS).

It’s not a disorder, but it is associated with deeper emotional processing, heightened awareness, and a more reactive nervous system.

Brain imaging shows that people high in SPS have stronger activity in regions involved in empathy, emotion, and decision-making. Your system is wired to take in more and feel it more intensely.

That same sensitivity makes you more attuned to pressure, people’s expectations, and your own self-criticism.

You often over-prepare, overthink, and over-function, because it helps you feel a little more in control.

You look capable on the outside, but your nervous system is constantly scanning for “what could go wrong.”

That’s high functioning anxiety, a pattern of coping that keeps you going, even when you feel on edge.

Many HSPs also relate to ADHD or autism traits like sensory overwhelm, emotional intensity, and need for routine. These experiences often co-occur, especially in women.

How to stop spiralling after you make a mistake
(There’s a scientific reason your brain won’t let you stop thinking about it)

Your brain isn’t replaying the mistake because you’re “dramatic.”

It’s replaying it because your nervous system is trying to protect you from rejection, embarrassment or disapproval.

For highly sensitive women, mistakes can feel emotionally unsafe.

So your brain keeps scanning:

* “How bad was it?”
* “Are they upset with me?”
* “What if I ruined everything?”

But overthinking is not resolution.

It’s threat monitoring.

What actually helps?

Pause before overexplaining.
Stop trying to get certainty immediately.
Let your body calm down before analysing the situation.
And remember:

Someone judging you or misunderstanding you is painful.

But it is not survival.

High sensitivity is linked to a temperament trait called sensory processing sensitivity (SPS).

It’s not a disorder, but it is associated with deeper emotional processing, heightened awareness, and a more reactive nervous system.

Brain imaging shows that people high in SPS have stronger activity in regions involved in empathy, emotion, and decision-making. Your system is wired to take in more and feel it more intensely.

That same sensitivity makes you more attuned to pressure, people’s expectations, and your own self-criticism.

You often over-prepare, overthink, and over-function, because it helps you feel a little more in control.

You look capable on the outside, but your nervous system is constantly scanning for “what could go wrong.”

That’s high functioning anxiety, a pattern of coping that keeps you going, even when you feel on edge.

Many HSPs also relate to ADHD or autism traits like sensory overwhelm, emotional intensity, and need for routine. These experiences often co-occur, especially in women.

Your body listens to sensation, not pressure. It’s trying to protect you. Stop forcing calm. Start showing it safety.

	1.	Hum everything. Shower, walk, or clean…just hum. The vibration hits your vagus nerve. It’s a physical ‘off switch’ for stress.

	2.	The 30-second shake. Shake your hands and legs. Stress lives in your muscles. Animals shake to reset, you should too. Discharge the energy.

	3.	The self-anchor. Hand on heart, hand on belly. Breathe. Physical touch signals safety faster than any thought can.

	4.	Feel the floor. Press your feet hard into the ground. Feel the floor push back. It tells your nervous system: “I am here. I am solid.”

	5.	Say the words. Say it or write it: “I am safe right now.” You don’t have to believe it. Just acknowledge the fact of this moment.

You don’t need to do this perfectly. Remember that your body is not your enemy. Start small. You are doing enough.

We’ve all been there, that moment when you want to calm down, but your body just won’t cooperate. Your heart is racing, your breathing feels strange, your thoughts are spiraling, and it leaves you wondering why you can’t control it.⁠
⁠
What’s actually happening is that your nervous system has switched into survival mode. It believes there’s a threat, even if you’re physically safe. To protect you, your body speeds up your heart to deliver oxygen faster, changes your breathing to support action, redirects blood away from digestion and the skin, and prepares your muscles to respond.⁠
⁠
This is why anxiety can come with dizziness, chest tightness, sweating, nausea, shaking, or a feeling of being disconnected. These sensations feel intense and uncomfortable, but they aren’t dangerous. They’re signs that your body is doing what it was designed to do...keep you alive.⁠
Understanding what’s happening doesn’t make anxiety disappear instantly, but it can make it feel less frightening. ⁠

Hard conversations go well when your body is calm, not when your script is perfect.⁠
⁠
Regulate first. Slow your breathing, settle your shoulders, and wait until your nervous system is steady. If you’re agitated, they will feel it too.⁠
⁠
Then speak in I-statements instead of you-statements.⁠
It keeps the other person’s defences down and opens the door for real listening.⁠
⁠
Try: “I felt…” “I need…” “I’m hoping we can…”⁠
⁠
Go in knowing your why.⁠
Why does this matter? What happens if nothing changes? Is that sustainable for you?⁠
⁠
And if you lose your calm mid-conversation, pause.⁠
⁠
Come back when your body is regulated again.⁠
⁠
Honesty is a must during hard conversations but so is staying grounded enough to be heard. ⁠

If that sounds like your situation, you might be experiencing burnout. ⁠
⁠
Burnout encompasses a wide range of symptoms affecting your physical, mental, and emotional health as a result of ongoing stress and overextending yourself. It is now accepted by health professionals as a medical diagnosis. ⁠
⁠
Left unaddressed burnout can cause anxiety, depression, cardiovascular disease, and poor emotional health, negatively affecting your ability to solve problems, think creatively, and utilize your working memory. ⁠
⁠
Which Type of Burnout Are You Experiencing?⁠
⁠
Read through the two types of burnout to decipher which best describes your situation. ⁠
⁠
1. Overload Burnout⁠
Perhaps the most familiar type, overload burnout stems from relentless striving for success. If you find yourself often feeling testy and neglecting your relationships, your health, and your life outside of work for your career, you may be in the throes of overload burnout. ⁠
⁠
2. Under-challenge Burnout⁠
On the other side of the spectrum, this type of burnout results from a lack of stimulation in your job. You wind up feeling apathetic and doing the bare minimum to continue getting by at work. The absence of passion or purpose causes you to detach from your job, which further fuels the cycle of feeling chronically underwhelmed by your work life. ⁠
⁠

A guide for people who feel things deeply ⬇️ 

Your intense emotions are never the problem ❤️ …what you do with them is.

Being someone who feels deeply is your superpower.
You have the capacity to tune into life in ways others can’t.
But it can feel overwhelming.

You don’t have to “toughen up” or “get over it.”
You can honor your emotions without being controlled by them.

Imagine this…

You feel intense emotions, but instead of spiraling and doing something out of character, you feel grounded, calm, and in control.

That’s emotional mastery.

Emotional mastery isn’t about ignoring or numbing your feelings.

It’s about learning to ride the waves, instead of being swept away by them.

Action Step 1: Acknowledge the emotion
Start by naming what you’re feeling.
Simply saying, “I feel angry” or “I feel sad” takes away its power to control you.

Action Step 2: Ground yourself in the present
Place your hand on your heart, take a deep breath, and remind yourself…

“I am safe right now.”
This helps your nervous system settle.

Action Step 3: Move the energy
Feelings are energy in motion.
Go for a walk, stretch, or shake it out.
Moving your body helps process the emotion instead of letting it stay stuck.

Action Step 4: Bring in compassion
Talk to yourself the way you’d talk to a friend.
It’s okay to feel deeply.
Your emotions don’t define you, but they do need your kindness.

Mastering your emotions isn’t about suppressing them, it’s about transforming how you respond.

The more you practice, the more power you gain over how you feel… no matter how intense it gets.

I stop overthinking in its tracks ⬇️⬇️⬇️

As a highly sensitive person I feel EVERYTHING deeply, and I spent years trying to avoid difficult feelings, because let’s face it, they feel awful. 

BUT in trying to avoid the anxiety I felt when I didn’t have control over a situation, or I didn’t think it would pan out the way I wanted (causing more difficult feelings)…

I was creating unhelpful coping strategies + teaching myself that difficult feelings are bad, so I must do whatever I could to get rid of them. 

Enter…overthinking, catastrophising + avoidance. 

(I really thought overthinking a problem was doing something).

The truth..

Only solving a problem is doing something. +
Worrying or catastrophising actually diminishes your ability to problem solve effectively…..

So, when my brain gets into anxious spiral mode heres a little trick I use to help me get out of it. 

⬇️

1. I write the anxious thought down and schedule a time to come back to it later in the day. This is my ‘worry time’. 

If I have any more anxious type thoughts I write them down as well, and come back to them at the worry time. 

2. Whilst I’m waiting for my worry time…

I give my  mind something else to anchor it’s attention to. 

Like my breathing, or sounds I can hear, or the colours on a TV show, or what I can feel in my body. I use as many of my 5 senses as poss.

3. When my worry time comes up, I worry until my hearts content. I usually find that the thing I was anxious about isn’t an issue anymore, and if it is, no worries.

Now I have a chance at solving it. 

All the while I’m sitting with the difficult feeling (they will still be there) and delighting in the opportunity to get acquainted with it. 

It might not work for everyone, but it works for me.

 No time to walk?…

When it pops up, say..

Then turn your attention to something else.

This trains your brain to deprioritise the memory.

How I stop overthinking in its tracks ⬇️⬇️⬇️

As a highly sensitive person I feel EVERYTHING deeply, and I spent years trying to avoid difficult feelings, because let’s face it, they feel awful. 

BUT in trying to avoid the anxiety I felt when I didn’t have control over a situation, or I didn’t think it would pan out the way I wanted (causing more difficult feelings)…

I was creating unhelpful coping strategies + teaching myself that difficult feelings are bad, so I must do whatever I could to get rid of them. 

Enter…overthinking, catastrophising + avoidance. 

(I really thought overthinking a problem was doing something).

The truth..

Only solving a problem is doing something. +
Worrying or catastrophising actually diminishes your ability to problem solve effectively…..

So, when my brain gets into anxious spiral mode heres a little trick I use to help me get out of it. 

⬇️

1. I write the anxious thought down and schedule a time to come back to it later in the day. This is my ‘worry time’. 

If I have any more anxious type thoughts I write them down as well, and come back to them at the worry time. 

2. Whilst I’m waiting for my worry time…

I give my  mind something else to anchor it’s attention to. 

Like my breathing, or sounds I can hear, or the colours on a TV show, or what I can feel in my body. I use as many of my 5 senses as poss.

3. When my worry time comes up, I worry until my hearts content. I usually find that the thing I was anxious about isn’t an issue anymore, and if it is, no worries.

Now I have a chance at solving it. 

All the while I’m sitting with the difficult feeling (they will still be there) and delighting in the opportunity to get acquainted with it. 

It might not work for everyone, but it works for me.

Rotating a few of the same corporate on top, coach potato on the bottom pieces of clothing.

Most importantly…

Now I just make the decision and assess the outcome. 

As for you my love, trust yourself.

Remember that your recovery game from any bad decision is A1.

Yes, these behaviour can come across as rude there is no denying this. However, like with all behaviour, it comes from somewhere....⁠⁠

In this case many of these behaviours are what we call safety behaviours (lack of eye contact, for example), and some are full blown avoidance (cancelling plans, not responding to texts). ⁠⁠
⁠⁠
Both safety behaviours and avoidance are designed to keep the anxious person safe from what they consciously or subconsciously perceive as a threatening situation. ⁠⁠
⁠⁠
Now you might think well its just a conversation where’s the threat? 

But if you’re a person that thinks people are constantly judging you, or that you will mess up, say something wrong and completely embarrass yourself and never be able to live it down, then yes, a simple conversation can be a threat. ⁠⁠
⁠⁠
The problem with avoidance and safety behaviours? ⁠⁠
⁠⁠
They are actually two of the biggest things that maintain anxiety. 

Yes, they relieve a little anxiety in the short term but that leads you to become more and more reliant on them. 

What happens then? 

Well, you need to face your fears in order to get over them and feel confident, but you cant face your fears if you are avoiding them. Thus the anxiety remains.⁠⁠

Which type of burnout are you experiencing? 

I see you. You’ve invested long hours and late nights into your profession and you’ve made incredible progress. 

However, instead of feeling proud of your accomplishments and optimistic about what’s to come, you’re constantly exhausted, feeling at the end of your rope and hopeless. ⁠
⁠
If that sounds like your situation, you might be experiencing burnout. ⁠
⁠
Burnout encompasses a wide range of symptoms affecting your physical, mental, and emotional health as a result of ongoing stress and overextending yourself. It is now accepted by health professionals as a medical diagnosis. ⁠
⁠
Left unaddressed burnout can cause anxiety, depression, cardiovascular disease, and poor emotional health, negatively affecting your ability to solve problems, think creatively, and utilize your working memory. ⁠
⁠
Which Type of Burnout Are You Experiencing?⁠
⁠
Read through the two types of burnout to decipher which best describes your situation. ⁠
⁠
1. Overload Burnout⁠
Perhaps the most familiar type, overload burnout stems from relentless striving for success. If you find yourself often feeling testy and neglecting your relationships, your health, and your life outside of work for your career, you may be in the throes of overload burnout. ⁠
⁠
2. Under-challenge Burnout⁠
On the other side of the spectrum, this type of burnout results from a lack of stimulation in your job. You wind up feeling apathetic and doing the bare minimum to continue getting by at work. The absence of passion or purpose causes you to detach from your job, which further fuels the cycle of feeling chronically underwhelmed by your work life. ⁠
⁠
I hope this helps give a little clarity.⁠

⁠⁠
Yes, these behaviour can ‘come across as rude’ there is no denying this. However, like with all behaviour, it comes from somewhere....⁠⁠
⁠⁠
In this case many of these behaviours are what we call safety behaviours (lack of eye contact, for example), and some are full blown avoidance (cancelling plans, not responding to texts). ⁠⁠
⁠⁠
Both safety behaviours and avoidance are designed to keep the anxious person safe from what they consciously or subconsciously perceive as a threatening situation. ⁠⁠
⁠⁠
Now you might think well its just a conversation where’s the threat? 

But if you’re a person that thinks people are constantly judging you, or that you will mess up, say something wrong and completely embarrass yourself and never be able to live it down, then yes, a simple conversation can be a threat. ⁠⁠
⁠⁠
The problem with avoidance and safety behaviours? ⁠⁠
⁠⁠
They are actually two of the biggest things that maintain anxiety. 

Yes, they relieve a little anxiety in the short term but that leads you to become more and more reliant on them. 

What happens then? 

Well, you need to face your fears in order to get over them and feel confident, but you cant face your fears if you are avoiding them. Thus the anxiety remains.⁠⁠

How to cut through the noise of overthinking ⬇️

Up until the last few years my day to day life was a struggle. On the outside I was an NHS Clinical Psychologist…a doctor, with two degrees! but on the inside it felt like highly sensitive mayhem. 

The high functioning anxiety was constant. The self doubt, crippling. My thoughts felt like a runaway train from morning to night. 

I felt pulled every which way, struggling to make decisions. Everything felt like a priority. Feeling guilty for saying no.

By the end of every week I was exhausted and spent most weekends in bed, laptop open, but in freeze mode! 

Now I feel more at peace & purposeful than I ever imagined. 

Here are three of the most impactful things I did 

1. Became my own cheerleader by developing my self compassion skills. 

2. Started somatic practice to regulate my threat response. 

3. Created a clear direction for myself via crystal clear values based goals. 

Goals for my life that were so in alignment with me, not what society told me I should be, that every step of the journey felt meaningful. Even when it felt hard. 

Because I knew exactly what I wanted my professional (and personal)  life to look like, making decisions became very easy + Knowing where to, and where not to focus my attention became very easy.

I don’t feel scattered because I have 1 direction & I know how to stay on track. 

Here are the first 3 steps to creating value based goals. 

1. Define/redefine your values -  what’s meaningful to you. How you want to show up in all the core areas of your life (health, career, relationships etc). You will have different values for different areas of life.

2. Create SMART goals in line with those values - they should be specific, meaningful, adaptive, realistic, & time bound. You will have different goals for different areas of your life.

3. Identify any obstacles that might stand in the way - thoughts, feelings, resources etc.

Self care tips ⬇️⬇️

One of THE most important self care strategies, 
(yes I’m calling it a strategy because consistent self care requires deliberate planning, execution and problem solving)…Is setting boundaries with yourself and others. 

Boundaries that serve a clear purpose, aren’t wishy washy, but not so rigid that you create more issues for yourself. 

The boundaries you need to set will vary depending on who you are, the people you have in your space, how you spend your time and what you’re trying to achieve. Think time boundaries, emotional boundaries etc. 

But as a start try these journaling prompts to get thinking about where boundaries might be helpful in improving your quality of life. 

1. In my life, people are not allowed to…

2. I have a right to…

3. To protect my time and energy, I’m allowed to…

Quick tip: I usually set 5 minutes a day aside for journaling. Any longer than that and I always manage to put it off.

A N X I E T Y at night is the worst right?⁠
⁠
⁠🎨kaydenhines⁠
⁠
So you’re literally in your bed all cosied up, away from the stress of the world☺️ and BAM - your brain lights up and finds itself ruminating about and every worry you held off during the day… Bye bye sleep.⁠
⁠
You would think that being far away from your boss, not dealing with commuters, not having anyone to answer to but yourself would trigger rest right? 

Not always, anxiety being manageable during the day then coming in like a ton of bricks once you’re winding down at night is a super-common experience. 

For a lot of us it’s basically the first time we’re first alone with our , so what happens? The entire day’s worth of thoughts come into your mind, which causes a level of anxiety.⁠💭💭💭😑⁠
⁠
Ironically sleep deprivation can be a trigger for anxiety during the day. So anxiety can cause sleep deprivation and sleep deprivation influences anxiety (how cruel is that)😤. 

This is just not sustainable and to combat the anxiety—and it helps to start preparing hours before you hit the sheets, then focus on calming your body down once you do🤗 . ⁠
⁠
Now is still a VERY stressful time for many of us but you can’t ignore your stress and anxiety all day long and expect it to magically disappear at bedtime, so throughout the day and in the evening carve out time for⁠
⁠
🌿 Relaxation exercises (belly breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, imagery)⁠
⁠
🌿Mindfulness meditation (try headspace)⁠
⁠
🌿Mind-body exercise (yoga etc)⁠
⁠
🌿Sleep hygiene is also extremely important (check my story highlights for lots of sleep hygiene tips)⁠

⁠

⁠
The faster you decide, the quicker you soar. ⁠

I see you. You’ve invested long hours and late nights into your profession and you’ve made incredible progress. 

However, instead of feeling proud of your accomplishments and optimistic about what’s to come, you’re constantly exhausted, feeling at the end of your rope and hopeless. ⁠
⁠
If that sounds like your situation, you might be experiencing burnout. ⁠
⁠
Burnout encompasses a wide range of symptoms affecting your physical, mental, and emotional health as a result of ongoing stress and overextending yourself. It is now accepted by health professionals as a medical diagnosis. ⁠
⁠
Left unaddressed burnout can cause anxiety, depression, cardiovascular disease, and poor emotional health, negatively affecting your ability to solve problems, think creatively, and utilize your working memory. ⁠
⁠
Which Type of Burnout Are You Experiencing?⁠
⁠
Read through the two types of burnout to decipher which best describes your situation. ⁠
⁠
1. Overload Burnout⁠
Perhaps the most familiar type, overload burnout stems from relentless striving for success. If you find yourself often feeling testy and neglecting your relationships, your health, and your life outside of work for your career, you may be in the throes of overload burnout. ⁠
⁠
2. Under-challenge Burnout⁠
On the other side of the spectrum, this type of burnout results from a lack of stimulation in your job. You wind up feeling apathetic and doing the bare minimum to continue getting by at work. The absence of passion or purpose causes you to detach from your job, which further fuels the cycle of feeling chronically underwhelmed by your work life. ⁠
⁠

High Functioning Anxiety is the experience of high levels of anxiety and the physical symptoms that come with it BUT seemingly functioning well (like really really well) in your day-to-day life. 

Doctors cannot diagnose high functioning anxiety because it is not a recognized disorder YET, making it difficult to get the appropriate treatment but the symptoms are VERY real…

Worry, fear, and anxiety
An inability to relax
A need for perfectionism
Overachieving/Overfunctioning
Fear of failure or judgment
A desire to keep busy all the time
Overthinking and overanalyzing
Anxiety before events
Elevated heart rate and faster breathing
Sleep problems
Digestive issues

Research suggests that in general anxiety disorders most likely occur due to a combination of factors, such as…

Exposure to stress: Experiencing stress or trauma at ANY point can trigger ongoing anxiety.

Genetics: People with a family history of anxiety disorders or other mental health conditions are more likely than others to develop anxiety and not just because of the environmental factors.

Personality: Traits of high sensitivity or nervousness in new situations, for example, increase the risk of having an anxiety disorder.

Health issues: Underlying physical health concerns, such as a thyroid disorder or heart problems can trigger or worsen anxiety symptoms. 

Drug or alcohol use: Misuse of drugs or alcohol can trigger anxiety, as can withdrawal from these substances.

Taking a holistic approach is key when treating high functioning anxiety. 

In my clinical practice I have seen a combination of cognitive, behavioural, and somatic approaches work best.

In this case many of these behaviours are what we call safety behaviours (lack of eye contact, for example), and some are full blown avoidance (cancelling plans, not responding to texts). ⁠⁠
⁠⁠
Both safety behaviours and avoidance are designed to keep the anxious person safe from what they consciously or subconsciously perceive as a threatening situation. ⁠⁠
⁠⁠
Now you might think well its just a conversation where’s the threat? 

But if you’re a person that thinks people are constantly judging you, or that you will mess up, say something wrong and completely embarrass yourself and never be able to live it down, then yes, a simple conversation can be a threat. ⁠⁠
⁠⁠
The problem with avoidance and safety behaviours? ⁠⁠
⁠⁠
They are actually two of the biggest things that maintain anxiety. 

Yes, they relieve a little anxiety in the short term but that leads you to become more and more reliant on them. 

What happens then? 

Well, you need to face your fears in order to get over them and feel confident, but you cant face your fears if you are avoiding them. Thus the anxiety remains.⁠⁠

Step 1.

Everyone tells you to ‘feel your emotions’ but what if you struggle to know how you feel?

If you find it hard to put words to your emotions you’re not alone. 

But not having the language to explain how you feel can make difficult emotions like anxiety, anger, sadness and guilt feel worse.

If we don’t have the skills to regulate our emotions we end up doing things (unhelpful things) to get rid of them. 

This can range from overthinking, and people pleasing, all the way to murder! …I’m not even being dramatic.

Here’s the thing…

- Growing up you probably didn’t attend ‘emotion regulation’ lessons at school. That wasn’t a thing.

You probably just did whatever you could to make difficult emotions go away, including pushing them down.

- Maybe ignoring your emotions was the best way for you to cope with being in an emotionally invalidating environment.

- Maybe you’re a a highly sensitive person, and constantly being told you were ‘too sensitive’ when you reacted to being hurt, probably made you feel like anything you ‘felt’ was wrong.

Whatever the reason there’s no judgement, you’re not defective, and there are ways that you can learn to increase your emotional vocabulary, and your emotion regulation skills.

Step 1. Make a habit of noticing when you feel ‘something’.

Step 2. Try to name what you’re feeling. Anxious? Angry? Sad? All of it?

Step 3. Identify what might be triggering this feeling. Current situation? The past? A misinterpretation?

Step 4. 🔑 Allow the feeling to be there and get really curious about it - Where in your body can you feel it?

Try and describe it as if you were a curious scientist whose never felt anything like this before and is entirely fascinated by it 

(Don’t forget to breathe)

And remember your emotions can never get bigger than you.

Pause and ask…Am I hearing their words… or my wounds?
That question changed everything for me. 

I never used to listen to understand, I listened through my triggers.

When someone said something that hit a nerve, my nervous system reacted before I even processed the words. 

Now all of a sudden, I wasn’t responding to them, I was responding to every moment I’d felt dismissed, disrespected, judged, or not good enough.

I started hearing things like…

“They’re criticising me.”
“They don’t see how much I do.”
“They’re trying to manipulate me.”

Defences up.

This continued until I started asking myself

But what if… they weren’t?

What if my reaction wasn’t proof of their intention, but a sign of an unhealed wound?

I started listening with my ears. 

Listening with your ears means staying grounded in the now, not your past.

Asking if this really about them? Or am I reacting to something I’ve felt before?

That’s emotional maturity.

Try this super simple technique straight from the Acceptance and Commitment Therapy model (my fave)…

The “I just had the thought that” technique. 

Next time an unwelcome thought pops up, acknowledge it by saying, “I just had the thought that [insert your thought here].” 

This simple shift puts space between you and the thought, helping you see it for what it is—a thought, not a fact. 

It’s based on the science of cognitive defusion, aiming to lessen the grip of intrusive thoughts by changing how you relate to them. 

Cognitive diffusion helps unhook you from the thought’s emotional undercurrent, redirecting your attention to what truly matters.

That’s exactly what I help you do inside my High-Functioning Anxiety Program.

I see you. You’ve invested long hours and late nights into your profession and you’ve made incredible progress. 

However, instead of feeling proud of your accomplishments and optimistic about what’s to come, you’re constantly exhausted, feeling at the end of your rope and hopeless. ⁠
⁠
If that sounds like your situation, you might be experiencing burnout. ⁠
⁠
Burnout encompasses a wide range of symptoms affecting your physical, mental, and emotional health as a result of ongoing stress and overextending yourself. It is now accepted by health professionals as a medical diagnosis. ⁠
⁠
Left unaddressed burnout can cause anxiety, depression, cardiovascular disease, and poor emotional health, negatively affecting your ability to solve problems, think creatively, and utilize your working memory. ⁠
⁠
Which Type of Burnout Are You Experiencing?⁠
⁠
Read through the two types of burnout to decipher which best describes your situation. ⁠
⁠
1. Overload Burnout⁠
Perhaps the most familiar type, overload burnout stems from relentless striving for success. If you find yourself often feeling testy and neglecting your relationships, your health, and your life outside of work for your career, you may be in the throes of overload burnout. ⁠
⁠
2. Under-challenge Burnout⁠
On the other side of the spectrum, this type of burnout results from a lack of stimulation in your job. You wind up feeling apathetic and doing the bare minimum to continue getting by at work. The absence of passion or purpose causes you to detach from your job, which further fuels the cycle of feeling chronically underwhelmed by your work life. ⁠
⁠

How I dealt with feeling like an imposter. ⁠
⁠
🎨crazyheadcomics⁠ great graphic inspired me to repost my experiences of feeling like an imposter 👇🏾
⁠
Despite having two degrees I spent ALOT of time feeling as though I wasn’t as competent or intelligent as others might think—and that soon enough, people would discover the ‘truth’ about me. ⁠
⁠
I managed to gain a place on clinical training and complete a doctorate but I still felt like a fraud. Instead of acknowledging my capabilities and my efforts I put it all down to luck and good timing. ⁠
⁠
And I know it’s not just me...⁠
⁠
Research suggests that around 25 to 30 percent of people that seem like high achievers may suffer from imposter syndrome. And around 70 percent of adults may experience ‘impostorism’ at least once in their lifetime. ⁠
⁠
When anyone would call attention to my success, or if I would pass an exam or get promoted, imposter syndrome would make its grand entrance. ⁠
⁠
My friends and family would proudly say “Meet Michaela, she’s a doctor”, and inside I would be screaming ‘noooooo don’t tell them that, they’re going to expect me to be smart!!!’.⁠
⁠
I felt pressure to perform at my absolute best 100 percent of the time, and when I didnt, I felt incompetent and anxious. ⁠
⁠
BUT....⁠
⁠
I knew that if I was going to be able to live a content, meaningful, balanced, valued based life I had to shake it. ⁠
⁠
🌟The biggest shift for me came from the following things:⁠
⁠
🌟Learning to tolerate discomfort and accept my imperfections.⁠
⁠
🌟Making sure I constantly acknowledging my expertise and accomplishments and always remind myself that wherever I am in life I earned it. I truly became my own cheerleader.⁠
⁠
🌟No longer comparing myself to others. ⁠
⁠
🌟No longer putting pressure on myself to complete every task flawlessly⁠
⁠
I am a work in progress, a ‘wounded healer’ if you will. I acknowledge that I am both amazing and flawed and I have no shame in either.

I see you. You’ve invested long hours and late nights into your profession and you’ve made incredible progress. 

However, instead of feeling proud of your accomplishments and optimistic about what’s to come, you’re constantly exhausted, feeling at the end of your rope and hopeless. ⁠
⁠
If that sounds like your situation, you might be experiencing burnout. ⁠
⁠
Burnout encompasses a wide range of symptoms affecting your physical, mental, and emotional health as a result of ongoing stress and overextending yourself. It is now accepted by health professionals as a medical diagnosis. ⁠
⁠
Left unaddressed burnout can cause anxiety, depression, cardiovascular disease, and poor emotional health, negatively affecting your ability to solve problems, think creatively, and utilize your working memory. ⁠
⁠
Which Type of Burnout Are You Experiencing?⁠
⁠
Read through the two types of burnout to decipher which best describes your situation. ⁠
⁠
1. Overload Burnout⁠
Perhaps the most familiar type, overload burnout stems from relentless striving for success. If you find yourself often feeling testy and neglecting your relationships, your health, and your life outside of work for your career, you may be in the throes of overload burnout. ⁠
⁠
2. Under-challenge Burnout⁠
On the other side of the spectrum, this type of burnout results from a lack of stimulation in your job. You wind up feeling apathetic and doing the bare minimum to continue getting by at work. The absence of passion or purpose causes you to detach from your job, which further fuels the cycle of feeling chronically underwhelmed by your work life. ⁠
⁠
I hope this helps give a little clarity.⁠
⁠
All my love ⁠

I see you. You’ve invested long hours and late nights into your profession and you’ve made incredible progress. 

However, instead of feeling proud of your accomplishments and optimistic about what’s to come, you’re constantly exhausted, feeling at the end of your rope and hopeless. ⁠
⁠
If that sounds like your situation, you might be experiencing burnout. ⁠
⁠
Burnout encompasses a wide range of symptoms affecting your physical, mental, and emotional health as a result of ongoing stress and overextending yourself. It is now accepted by health professionals as a medical diagnosis. ⁠
⁠
Left unaddressed burnout can cause anxiety, depression, cardiovascular disease, and poor emotional health, negatively affecting your ability to solve problems, think creatively, and utilize your working memory. ⁠
⁠
Which Type of Burnout Are You Experiencing?⁠
⁠
Read through the two types of burnout to decipher which best describes your situation. ⁠
⁠
1. Overload Burnout⁠
Perhaps the most familiar type, overload burnout stems from relentless striving for success. If you find yourself often feeling testy and neglecting your relationships, your health, and your life outside of work for your career, you may be in the throes of overload burnout. ⁠
⁠
2. Under-challenge Burnout⁠
On the other side of the spectrum, this type of burnout results from a lack of stimulation in your job. You wind up feeling apathetic and doing the bare minimum to continue getting by at work. The absence of passion or purpose causes you to detach from your job, which further fuels the cycle of feeling chronically underwhelmed by your work life. ⁠
⁠
I hope this helps give a little clarity.⁠

I see you. You’ve invested long hours and late nights into your profession and you’ve made incredible progress. 

However, instead of feeling proud of your accomplishments and optimistic about what’s to come, you’re constantly exhausted, feeling at the end of your rope and hopeless. ⁠
⁠
If that sounds like your situation, you might be experiencing burnout. ⁠
⁠
Burnout encompasses a wide range of symptoms affecting your physical, mental, and emotional health as a result of ongoing stress and overextending yourself. It is now accepted by health professionals as a medical diagnosis. ⁠
⁠
Left unaddressed burnout can cause anxiety, depression, cardiovascular disease, and poor emotional health, negatively affecting your ability to solve problems, think creatively, and utilize your working memory. ⁠
⁠
Which Type of Burnout Are You Experiencing?⁠
⁠
Read through the two types of burnout to decipher which best describes your situation. ⁠
⁠
1. Overload Burnout⁠
Perhaps the most familiar type, overload burnout stems from relentless striving for success. If you find yourself often feeling testy and neglecting your relationships, your health, and your life outside of work for your career, you may be in the throes of overload burnout. ⁠
⁠
2. Under-challenge Burnout⁠
On the other side of the spectrum, this type of burnout results from a lack of stimulation in your job. You wind up feeling apathetic and doing the bare minimum to continue getting by at work. The absence of passion or purpose causes you to detach from your job, which further fuels the cycle of feeling chronically underwhelmed by your work life. ⁠
⁠
I hope this helps give a little clarity.⁠

I see you. You’ve invested long hours and late nights into your profession and you’ve made incredible progress. 

However, instead of feeling proud of your accomplishments and optimistic about what’s to come, you’re constantly exhausted, feeling at the end of your rope and hopeless. ⁠
⁠
If that sounds like your situation, you might be experiencing burnout. ⁠
⁠
Burnout encompasses a wide range of symptoms affecting your physical, mental, and emotional health as a result of ongoing stress and overextending yourself. It is now accepted by health professionals as a medical diagnosis. ⁠
⁠
Left unaddressed burnout can cause anxiety, depression, cardiovascular disease, and poor emotional health, negatively affecting your ability to solve problems, think creatively, and utilize your working memory. ⁠
⁠
Which Type of Burnout Are You Experiencing?⁠
⁠
Read through the two types of burnout to decipher which best describes your situation. ⁠
⁠
1. Overload Burnout⁠
Perhaps the most familiar type, overload burnout stems from relentless striving for success. If you find yourself often feeling testy and neglecting your relationships, your health, and your life outside of work for your career, you may be in the throes of overload burnout. ⁠
⁠
2. Under-challenge Burnout⁠
On the other side of the spectrum, this type of burnout results from a lack of stimulation in your job. You wind up feeling apathetic and doing the bare minimum to continue getting by at work. The absence of passion or purpose causes you to detach from your job, which further fuels the cycle of feeling chronically underwhelmed by your work life. ⁠
⁠
I hope this helps give a little clarity.⁠

Let me be clear, aiming for your best is awesome, but if you’re on an endless quest for absolute perfection you’re setting yourself up for a rollercoaster of shame, stress and self-doubt. ⁠

This can easily lead to procrastination and inaction. 
⁠
Your brain was designed to look for problems and solve them…

You have thousands of thoughts everyday and you can’t really stop all the negative thoughts that come to mind 

BUT…

You can choose what to do if negative thoughts arrive. 

So, instead of fighting, judging or acting on your perfectionist thoughts, the first thing you can do is just notice them.
⁠
This pause will give you time to act in ways that align with what is important and most helpful, rather than being driven by the need to be perfect. ⁠
⁠
Because life isn’t about being flawless, that’s impossible…I believe it’s about being genuine and true to yourself regardless of the outcome.
